utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers for the Office of the Prosecution; lead counsel Jan Wubben will join us later in the day. With me today, co-counsel Mr. Gramsci di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't told us who will make place for Mr. Wubben. And good morning to you. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution. I'm Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones we represent Mr. Naser Oric. And we have our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam and good morning to you and your team. Preliminaries. I have my attention -- it has been brought to my attention that during the sitting of the 30th September, page 11690 of the transcript, lines 11 to 14, although I had stated that the exhibit referred to was D788, it went down in the transcript as D778. So that's just for the record. The transcript was in error and I'm registering that. All right. Any preliminaries, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: None from this side of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, how long do you think your cross-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning to Your Honours. I anticipate that I will take the first two sessions. Since this witness has covered a significant amount of information about matters relating to the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm just making it clear that we cannot stay here today because one of us needs to leave the Tribunal at 1.00 at the latest so we cannot sit here beyond 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind and try to expedite my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary we will have one break rather than two. If you think that you can still finish by 12.30, then we can have two breaks as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's see how it goes. I think -- we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Start. You're still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, good morning to you and this morning I'd like to first advise you that we are probably going to be running a little short on time and I do need to finish a significant amount of material -- cover a significant amount of material with you. So I'd ask you to keep your answers brief, possibly a yes-no answer where appropriate and if you need to explain further, you won't be prevented from doing that. You can do so. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I mispronounce any of the names and it doesn't seem clear to you, please just let me know and I'll spell them out to you, so just as a prelude to some of what I'll be talking about, names of individuals or places.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And at some point I will have you look at the map that you utilised yesterday. I believe it was Defence Exhibit 793 so we'll cover some of that -- some of the areas you discussed as well. But firstly I'd like to take you back to Prosecution Exhibit P90 which is where we ended yesterday and we were -- if I could have the usher's assistance in giving that to the witness and it's also on Sanction, Your Honour. We are going back to page 25 of the English version of the document and I believe we established yesterday that the B/C/S was located, I believe, on page 50, if I'm not mistaken. So perhaps you can go back to page 50 and again we are starting with the sentence that includes the name Seco, I'm not sure I'm pronouncing it right again. But it's Mr. Delic. Can you see that in your version?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday before the end of the session, there was a discussion about the translation of the English in comparison to the B/C/S version and, Your Honours, I believe you asked that we -- the Prosecution take a look at the translation to see if, in fact, there was some discrepancy. I can tell you this morning that there is some discrepancy and I think we will have to make efforts to resubmit a translation -- probably check the entire book again, and resubmit a translation if necessary. But with respect to this portion, there is some discrepancy. I was informed by our language assistant that the sentence, the first sentence should read, "on that occasion, 60 people had been killed, only Musan Talovic and Seco Delic escaped the death plan for them." (redacted)is it correct -- is this what the B/C/S version of the document states?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Seco Delic and he told me about this. As far as Musan Talovic is concerned, I know him but I don't know whether he was at this execution. He never told me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. But Mr. Delic told you that he had escaped -- that he had in effect not been executed as planned?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he also told you about Mr. Ibisevic and his two sons who had been killed with him, and that they had -- that they had been found embraced together?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me. I mean, he didn't tell me in the place where the execution took place but on the way from my house to that place where the execution took place, that's where I met him. When I came to the place where the execution took place, I saw Mustafa Ibisevic and his two sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Good enough. Now, if you read further in the document, there are the names mentioned of the various individuals, Serb individuals, who had been involved in the execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I will not read out the names for you from the book, from page 26, Your Honour, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But if you could look at those names that are stated, could you just tell us, with a yes or no, whether the names are the individuals that you were told were involved in the executions?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that yesterday, he saw the people there, Mladjenovic, Najdan, close by Milo, Ribo, Djedura and Mr. Deronjic. He saw them nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So the names that are reflected in this book are accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's clearly a distortion of the evidence which he's just given. One of the names which we've just seen doesn't appear there and he hasn't confirmed all the names so, you know, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can go through them one by one and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the case. That's why I allowed Mr. Jones to object before the witness started giving his answer because I would have objected too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The two brothers that are mentioned, Nidjan and Milenko Madanovic [sic] from Hranca, were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Najdan. I mean, try -- again, repeat the names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were they -- were you told that they were at the executions?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Najdan Mladjenovic was there and that he was seen there. I didn't see anything about Milenko.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. What about Miladin Jokic and Radomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said about Jokic, that he was the main person, as far as confiscating weapons in Glogova and issuing the ultimatum and already I talked about what he participated in and where he was seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about Radomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about Radomir Milosevic that he was killed. I think that he was killed on the 1st or the 2nd of June. That's when he was killed in Glogova and that he was found, meaning that he participated in the attack on Glogova and that he was killed on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So he participated on the attack. Was he also involved in the executions, that you know?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But the executions occurred on the first day of attack?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Let's take the next name, Radeno Milanovic [sic]. Do you know if he was involved?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say anything about this man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you don't know if he was involved? Do you know if he was involved, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, should I -- should she be asking me questions or should I be responding immediately after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't understand that. She asks you questions and unless I tell you, "Don't answer this question," you have to answer it. That's how it works here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you have an objection, you need to explain to us first and we will discuss amongst ourselves and we will see whether your objection is well-founded or not. Otherwise, she has -- she is doing her duty here. She has a very important responsibility before this Tribunal, and she must be allowed to make all the questions that the Prosecution feels are important, and you have a responsibility and an obligation to answer them. However, if there are questions that you find objection to, please address us. We are here to listen to everybody. And we will authorise you or not authorise you to refrain from answering, all right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So perhaps it's the case of repeating your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us if Mr. Pero Jovanovic was present. Let me just go back. There was one before, actually the first name that I wanted you to tell us about was Radeno Milanovic. Was he involved in the execution or involved in the attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know anything about that man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And what about Pero Jovanovic, from Hranca?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that man either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Tadija Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tadija, yes, I saw Tadija. Tadija was there. Maybe I didn't mention him yesterday but I saw him myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all the questions I have for now with respect to P90, and we'll get back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you had finished your cross-examination. I had already put on a smile on my face.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, we have a ways to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Let's go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to have interrupted you like this. But I know it's not your intention to create problems, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's also page 9, lines 7 to 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we were in private session then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I apologise to you for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us, tell the Trial Chamber, I believe you testified yesterday that you had not heard about -- heard of Naser Oric prior to August 8th. So just for clarification, was that after August 8, was that the first time you ever heard of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably after the 8th of August. I probably heard of him but the first time I met him was perhaps on the 10th or sometime between the 10th and the 15th of January, when I was in hospital in Srebrenica. That was the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And prior to August 8th, you never heard of him before?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't hear of him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you were in the hospital in Srebrenica, what did you hear of Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to the hospital. I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And what -- could you tell us about that? Did you speak with him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was seriously wounded. I was seriously wounded. I was in great pain. I just saw him pass by. We didn't talk, at least I don't remember us having talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And had you met him before?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I haven't met him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How did you know that was Oric, Naser Oric who passed you by in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, because I said I was in great pain, I think he was going from one hospital room to another, and one of the nurses may have mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you remember in what context she mentioned his name? Did she just say, "There goes Naser Oric," or was it in reference to something else, something in particular?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing specific. He was probably going to see the wounded, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how long -- how long a period of time when you saw him? Was he visiting individuals when you say he was probably visiting the wounded? Could you just explain a little bit more? Did you see him actually speaking with someone who was on a bed? You said he was going from room to room. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my room, there were four or five beds. I didn't see or notice him or talk with anyone since I was in great pain, I had an inflammation and my body temperature was high.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival in Srebrenica for the treatment, for medical treatment, what had you heard of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier, before I came there, I haven't heard of him, but perhaps later on I may have overheard a conversation concerning his name but nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who did you think Naser Oric was when the nurse pointed him out to you or mentioned that he was in the room?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he was an ordinary person like anyone else. All of the people there were the same. You couldn't distinguish one from another.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you later learn who he was? In terms of his position in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know what his function was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And no one told you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Because after three weeks in the hospital, I went back to Cizmici and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did the nurse point out anyone else to you other than Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people coming in and out all the time. I don't know who they or what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you don't know if he was in camouflage uniform or civilian clothing? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember that, his clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And you stated that there were other wounded men in the room with you. How many men were in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He already said there were five.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Is that correct? Sir? Five men?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, four or five.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And of those men, who were they? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't tell you their names because I didn't know them at the time and I was there briefly. I had my own problems and I left the hospital rather quickly and went back. Perhaps I would recognise them today but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And during this three weeks you were there, were these same men in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my own problems, as I said. I expected my arm to be cut off, and my body temperature was very high every day. I wasn't able to talk with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that these men were -- who were wounded, were fighters, such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were, whether they were wounded by grenades or shells. I think one of them was but I can't remember for others, for the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, you said that you didn't know them. You didn't know what areas of the Srebrenica region they were from? Or if in fact they were from Srebrenica, the Srebrenica region?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an individual named Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when did you hear of him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think after UNPROFOR entered Srebrenica, close to the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you learn what position, if any, he held in Srebrenica or in any other area in this -- in the region?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear the time that he was in any particular position or function. When UNPROFOR came in, and by mid-1993, I moved to Srebrenica because there was no more room in Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did you hear of him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also heard that his name was Zulfo Tursunovic and not much more, as well as any other ordinary person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you learn that he was one of the fighters in Srebrenica or had participated in defending the region?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I knew was that he was from the area of Suceska, nothing else. I had heard something before that, that he had some problems and probably that's why I remember him but that was prior to the war. It was unrelated to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that Suceska had a - excuse me - were you aware that Suceska had a Territorial Defence in May of - excuse me - in 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about Mirzet Halilovic? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you know Ahmo Tihic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ramiz Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Ramiz Becirovic perhaps in 1994, I think, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you know what position if any he held in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know concerning that period. I don't know if he held any function.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And before 1994, were you aware that Srebrenica had a Territorial Defence? Excuse me, I'll rephrase that question. Prior to your arrival in Srebrenica in January of 1993, were you aware that Srebrenica had a Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Muslims were in control of Srebrenica in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know precisely what was going on in Srebrenica but I knew that, since there are Pale and Potocari behind Cizmici, this is what I knew about. But as for the rest I didn't know anything about their activities and movements. So I knew that that part was free, towards Jaglici and Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And by free, meaning in control -- controlled by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you aware that these areas had Territorial Defence in them?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say they were free, what exactly do you mean? Free of Serbs as well? Not living in those areas?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Serbs lived there. I didn't know that part of the area. I got familiar with it later on, after UNPROFOR came to Srebrenica and into the area of Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that Serbs lived in Srebrenica prior to the out -- the conflict? Prior to May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. There were Serbs in Bratunac, in Srebrenica, but I didn't know precisely where and how many. I didn't know the same thing for the Muslims either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you -- was January of 1993, when you were treated in Srebrenica, was that the first time you'd been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you lived in Srebrenica, I believe you said from mid-1993, up until the fall of Srebrenica, 1995, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't there all of the time, since my mother was in Cizmici, and I would on occasion go to Cizmici and I spent my time in Srebrenica. So I was moving about the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. So you were able, from March of 1993 up until the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, to move between Srebrenica and Cizmici to visit your family?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you spent in Srebrenica, had you learned of Naser Oric's role in Srebrenica during 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You never -- did you speak to individuals who lived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you have in mind. I did speak with some people, but we couldn't discuss every single person in Srebrenica. There were 40.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And no one in Srebrenica during that time brought up the name of Naser Oric to you? And I'm talking about from March 1993 until 1995.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was of no importance. Why would anyone had to mention some names to me? I was just another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, you would agree, would you not, that individuals in Srebrenica at the time, when you were there, discussed various matters relating to what had occurred in the region in 1992 up until -- to the present, people talked about what was going on with the Serbs and the Muslims, did they not?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from different areas there, from four municipalities encompassing 400 villages. There were lots of people, and I can't remember exactly what the story and the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Did you talk about the liberation of the various areas in Srebrenica and Bratunac during the period of 1992 up until 1993?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mainly associated with people from Glogova. I spent my time with them and I would see them most often. I don't know what other people may have discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So is the answer to that question yes or no that you did not discuss with the people you knew about the liberation of Bratunac and Srebrenica -- and Srebrenica municipalities?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with all people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And no one ever mentioned the name Naser Oric to you in connection with the Srebrenica TO during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps people did mention Naser Oric's name but as to his position, that wasn't mentioned, and I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And when they mentioned his name, in what context did they mention his name?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the same as if they mentioned my name. There was nothing apart from the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, they just said the name and nothing else, who he was, what he was doing, was he in Srebrenica or not?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question since I already said what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. We can move on. Now, you mentioned yesterday that you were -- you had been a member of the antisabotage unit. Could you tell us -- and that was for a period of three months. Could you tell us some of the things that you did as a member of that unit? And this was during your training with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess we didn't understand each other too well. I said that in the former JNA, I was in the ABH branch, and after that, I underwent a three month training regarding the issue you mentioned but that wasn't at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clarifying that. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what types of activities, training, that you undertook as -- in this unit?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have the entire military term in mind or just the last three months?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about the last three months. In the antisabotage unit.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in or by the end of 1986, and at the beginning of 1987, I believe I went away at the beginning of 1987. So we had this antisabotage platoon and I was a member of the platoon. That was a three-month training. I don't know whether that was recorded anywhere but I did undergo the training. The place where I served my military was a hilly terrain, and since we have completed our nuclear, biological, chemical training we moved to another type of training, and for exercise, one group would be put on the top of a hill and then another group would be designated as well as their enemy, and it was our duty to locate them and to push them back, and we used blanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you all -- were you also trained in conducting reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know what a reconnaissance is?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose, and based on what I know what reconnoitring or doing reconnaissance is but apart from that I can't say much more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, why don't you tell us in your experience what that entails.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reconnaissance entails -- well, say, I had a pair of binoculars and I reconnoitre, doesn't matter who, but I want to learn of their movements, of their activities, I think that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it once you learn of their activities you're required to report the activities to someone.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I did the reconnaissance. I never said that. And I never said that I transferred any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No. I understand that. I'm just talking in general, once you reconnoitre an area, you should relay this information to a superior, should you not? Or someone who would consider this information of value?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, the scout would have to report to someone, it doesn't matter who, but we, for example, in our groups, we would have to tell at least one person and then they would pass on that information to others, as to what was happening in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We'll get back to that. Thank you. Yesterday, you testified that there were four armed groups, and that these groups were led by Ejub Golic. And that, in fact, these groups were located -- Your Honour, I see Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the transcript, he had -- the witness said a man who did the reconnaissance. He didn't use the word scout. He said the word, the man who reconnoitred, and we see here the word "scout" appearing. So the person observing. Then they would pass on the information, but he wasn't using the exact word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now that we are -- I thank you for the observation, Ms. Vidovic, and it is of some relevance for sure because throughout his entire examination-in-chief, the witness has been at least in -- as far as the transcript goes, I wasn't following his testimony in his own language, and I don't know which word he used in his own language, but as far as the transcript is concerned, I'm sure that we will find throughout the use of "scouts." He was testifying that they had their own scouts who were bringing information and they were sending scouts to forward information to others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour's recollection is correct and the transcript is replete with that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if the Defence think that is there is a difference between the use of the word "scout" and the use and the significance of the word that the witness may have been using, in his testimony during the examination-in-chief, please come forward and say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he kept saying, the man or a man doing reconnaissance. And this is different from the word "scout" which has a military sense to it. So a person observing. Witness, did you understand me? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also say, just so this doesn't get horribly confused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, and I would appreciate your intervention in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just to say, also we are talking about the evidence in chief and the evidence he just gave now, that the whole last bit of evidence about reconnaissance was, of course, about the JNA and in general matters what somebody doing reconnaissance does. He wasn't talking about the same thing as after 1992, so that should be clear to everyone as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just say, Your Honour, I think we can go back to the transcript. There was a point whether I asked the witness generally what reconnoiter entailed and then he said, when we did the -- when we in fact had someone do the reconnaissance, he used the word scout so I think that's not exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I -- usually I wouldn't have bothered about this but once you are American and you have knowledge of the American language. Mr. Jones is British and to us and to him and to me, scouts has quite a different connotation from a military -- I mean scouts for me is what I was in -- when I was a little boy. This is Lord Baden-Powell's organisation. So -- but I do understand that when he says or when I see in the transcript "scouts," is a person that is being given a particular task of reconnoitering, I mean, more or less. That's how I have understood it but I am not aware of the Serbo-Croat word that the witness used yesterday and the day before. I'm not aware of it. If there is the submission that the word that he used throughout these last two days has got a different significance to the word "scout" as it has appeared in the transcript and how I have said I understand it, then please tell us because we will rely on what we will have on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can ask the witness if there's a difference in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what word he used these last two days. Madam Vidovic can tell us which word he used or the transcript and the sound recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can ask the witness what word he used. Did he use the word "scout" or is he using the word, the person who did the reconnoitering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, these persons that were gathering information for you, bringing -- going out, gathering information and coming back and relaying it to you, which word did you use to describe them in your own language? I want the Serbo-Croat word from you. I want to hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A person, a person going somewhere who happened to have seen or observed something, a man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm at a loss. "Covjek," he said. "Covjek," he said. Is it important? I mean, I don't know. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's not important. I think we all understand what the witness is referring to, whether it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that these groups were located in Velika Glogova and Vladusici and Cizmici and they were led by Ejub Golic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that there was another group between Glogova and Vladusici, in the woods. That was the fourth group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So there was a total of four groups in all? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And they were all led by Ejub Golic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we got together and when we discussed the situation and that when we realised it was the last moment to do something, we agreed that he be the leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- and yesterday I know you had difficulties when I asked you how many men were in the groups -- and perhaps do you recall today how many men were in each group?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, people died every day. People got wounded every day. Every hour perhaps. So the manning strength varied. We never knew the precise number. We didn't have any lists, since we didn't have any paper, and we didn't have any time on our hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps the usher can assist me by showing the witness Defence Exhibit 809. One moment, Your Honour. Sorry, Your Honour, if I could have a moment. I apologise. I actually want -- as a matter of fact, sorry, Mr. Usher, if you can leave the witness with that document but I'd also like him to be shown Defence Exhibit 807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are keeping there 809?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's now being shown 807.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if you could just take a look at this document. Yesterday you recall that you were asked questions about certain information in the document. Now, I'm going to take you to the area which talks about the number of soldiers and the number of civilians and I will read from the English version. It's number 1, paragraph number 1, "We estimate that there are about 500 soldiers and a much larger number of civilians, 1.000 women and children, in this sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to say that fighters are also mentioned in the document and not soldiers, "borci" as opposed to "vojnici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So according to the Defence the translation in the English document text that you're using is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest that you read -- in any case, he is receiving interpretation in his own language. I want to make sure that he has received the correct word. Were you following Ms. Vidovic the proceedings in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's more that the Exhibit itself, D807 says soldiers and it's "borci."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I know, but what he is looking is not the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. It should be okay for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided you're happy with that, we can move ahead. Okay. All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just trying to determine who translated this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like the interpreters to follow the -- the interpreter again repeated that in the document it says "soldiers." In the Bosnian document, or in the document in Bosnian, it is said "fighters," "borci."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's borci that we are talking about and not soldiers. All right? Look at the document. The document that -- could you please -- usher, please put the document on the ELMO so that I make sure of what it says. And could we have the first paragraph zoomed in, please, enlarged? I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the first words on the fourth line, "borac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Borac, okay, yeah, all right. And those are fighters according to ... So we are -- it's borci that we are talking about, all right? In that document. Go ahead, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, you confirmed yesterday when you were asked about information in this document that there were a thousand women and children. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the document also states that we estimate that there were about 500 fighters and a much larger number of civilians and it goes on to talk about the number of civilians. Now I'd like to ask you about the number of fighters that is indicated here. Is that the number of fighters that were -- formed part of the groups that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. This is their estimate, the estimate of the person who drafted the report. Whether they were -- 500 soldiers there, I mean, the fighters, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But they estimated that --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it must mean that there were 500.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And they estimated the number of women and children, the civilians, correctly, as you confirmed?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I cannot, for the fighters, but as far as the civilians, there were about 1.000 to 1.500. That was always the number mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, speaking too fast. That's exactly what I'm asking. You confirm that the number they estimated of the women and children is correct. Just answer me with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the number of -- and they also estimate that there were 500 fighters in this document.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their estimate. It wasn't my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, what is your estimate, sir?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really wouldn't be able to say. Glogova is a broader area. I showed it to you yesterday. So there were no lists, there was nothing, and I cannot say how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done with that document for the moment. Thank you. Now, sir, you also testified yesterday when you were asked about the number of refugees in the area of Cizmici, you stated there were about 60, 80, or 90 or so living in the houses in Cizmici. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And that's a number you remember?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said about how many there were. I don't know if you understood properly that people were also living out in the open. They were outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question was with respect to your estimation of the number of civilians, so I believe you've answered correctly that you confirm that these were the numbers you were aware of in terms of the refugees in Cizmici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said yesterday that there were 60, 70, 80, or 90 in each house in Cizmici, not in houses in Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine and that's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is that you are very clear on the number of civilians that were in the area at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of Cizmici or Cizmici and Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cizmici. Could you please just clarify which period exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In July and August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late July and early August, there were about 1.000 to 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question is: How many fighters were there?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I've already said it, that I don't know how many fighters there were. I'm saying this for the 10th time, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were one of the fighters, correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just so that we understand, you're able to give us an estimate of the number of civilians but not of the number of fighters, of which -- of whom you were one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said -- well, let me say, for example, it's ranging from 300 to 400 men. This is my estimate though I don't know the exact number. I cannot state the exact number but I estimate that it was between 300 to 400.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We have one now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an objection. The witness did not at any point provide a correct or a precise estimate of the civilians. He's also saying between 1.000 to 1.500 civilians, and that cannot be considered as a precise number. That was just also an estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you are right. Basically we are talking about estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the same question, an estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can move. The whole idea behind your question was very obvious so let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I can move on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about Ejub Golic's leadership of the four groups during the period of may, June, July, up until August of 1992. You said that the four groups were located in four separate areas, in the area of Glogova. And at this time I'd like the usher's assistance with showing the witness Defence Exhibit 793. This is the map that you testified from yesterday, and you indicated a number of villages to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the ELMO in the way, Ms. Richardson? Can -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to find the areas that you were just testifying about, that the four groups were located. If you could just point to where those areas are so it could -- it will assist us in knowing exactly where the groups were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the colour? Because from the monitor you cannot tell exactly what the colour he used yesterday was and the day before. Could we give him another colour with which to indicate these spots, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's this map. I don't think it's on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think you have followed what I said. The markings that you are going to make now, I want them in a different colour from the ones -- from the one you used to mark the various places these last two days so that we can identify or distinguish these from the others. So what was the colour -- usher -- from where you are, what's the colour that he used?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Red. Could you now give him another colour, please? Yes. Now, Ms. Richardson wants you to indicate with spots, circles, on the map the four places where these four groups --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, I don't see Velika Glogova here. I think then that it was not this map. It was a different map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It is -- Velika Glogova is -- anyway, he is right. You can see Glogova there but that's Velika Glogova that you have on that map. We can get the other map, which was -- yes, that's the other map. We can get the other map. Would that be all right for you, Ms. Richardson, if he marks on the other map rather than on this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's take the other map and you mark on the other map. Thank you, sir, for pointing that out. So let's start. We want to know where these four places, where these four groups were stationed, where. I take it that one of them was Velika Glogova or -- but you know. Let's go through them one by one, the first --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Velika Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vladusici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one group was in between, here in the woods somewhere between Velika Glogova and Vladusici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you testified -- we can leave the map there for a moment. Perhaps, though, you can tell us how far Cizmici is -- how far away is Cizmici from Velika Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: About seven or eight kilometres. This is just my estimate. I don't know. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what about Glogova from Vlasucici?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladusici?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps two, 2.5 kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you also -- while you have -- while you have this map, could you also point to the area of Belicava? Do you see Belicava on the map? You can just point to it.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which area. I didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I can repeat it. Belicava. Or Beliceva?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bljeceva?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bljeceva is below. I don't have a marker.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part, below Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, you testified that Ejub Golic was the leader of all the four groups in these areas. Could you tell us how Ejub Golic communicated -- perhaps I should ask you this. I'll rephrase the question, sir. Where was Ejub Golic most of the time in May, June and July of 1992? Was he in one particular village? I believe you said it was Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. In Velika Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And he was able to communicate, as the leader of the group, with the group in Cizmici, seven to eight kilometres away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the area of Velika Glogova, and those people who comprised that group would come from those groups and there was talk about what was going on in the various places amongst the groups. So some people would come from a group and say that such and such a thing happened in that group and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. So someone -- so that I'm clear, someone from the Cizmici group would come to Velika Glogova to speak with Ejub Golic to report on what was happening in their group and in their area? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. [No interpretation]. It was most often through Mociva [phoen]; that was that connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you explain that? What do you mean it was most often through Mociva?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used that road, the people who were moving. They used the Cizmici-Mocila-Vladusici-Glogova road, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the best thing would be for the Prosecutor to repeat the question for the witness and for the witness to repeat the answer, because he did not mention Mocevici at all. He explained that way of communicating. Perhaps it would be good for the Prosecutor to repeat the question because there was no interpretation for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You mention that -- and if I did say the name Mocevici, it would be incorrect because I think the -- sir, you said it was Mocila?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mocila, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can do this. You mentioned that the people from Cizmici would communicate with Velika Glogova. Could you indicate on the map what path they would take? And that would probably hope us understand the road that you're talking about. And if you can use a marker so we'll have a record of that, thank you. Green is fine.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most frequently used was the Cizmici-Mocila road and they would reach Velika Glogova so that would be that road. I cannot really tell you precisely where they went. I can just give you the general direction. But only they know where they went, which paths they used, through which woods, along which creek, and so on they walked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did they come on -- was this journey on foot or other means of transportation? Did they use horses?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Only on foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what would they communicate to Ejub Golic, as the leader of the group, if you know? What types of things would they tell him about?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there with him every time. I was in the Velika Glogova area but I wasn't with him. They would more or less describe what the situation was where they were and then the others would say what the situation was in their terrain, and that's how the information was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This was done because the various members of the group would have someone reconnoiter the area?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who were moving in that terrain would often get killed on the road. I don't know whether it was because they ran into an ambush or stepped on a mine. There were all sorts of things happening. A person would go to convey something but they would never arrive. And the next person would go. And that person would then either get there or not get there. Some people managed to get to the place where they were going to and some did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was, though, the people from the group, for instance, Cizmici, the reason that they were able to communicate what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was going on in their area to Ejub Golic is because they had individuals who were observing what was -- what the Serbs were doing in the -- in the vicinity close to them. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They would survey the movements of the Serbs, where their artillery was located.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And with respect to your position in the Velika Glogova area, I take it you say you moved around a lot. Where exactly did you move around to? What areas?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Velika Glogova area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you go in the woods, where the other group was?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you go to --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Velika Glogova area is mostly a wooded area, maybe not 100 per cent, but about 60 to 70 per cent of the Velika Glogova territory is covered by woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you go to the other group in the location of Vladusici?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this -- all right. Thank you, and as you're moving around in this area, what was your function?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our function to repel any possible Serb attacks, which actually happened on a daily basis, and it was to fight. That was our function more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And would you consider your function, in terms of perhaps preventing the Serbs from entering this area, the Velika Glogova area, and the other areas where the groups were?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many men performed those duties along with you?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said several times that I didn't know the number, that the numbers changed from hour to hour, from day to day. People would be killed, wounded. It was always changing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you have a weapon during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, just you.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me recall when I managed to get ahold of a rifle. I think that it was sometime in late May, I think. I don't know the exact date, the exact period but I think it was sometime after the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I recall your testimony from yesterday that not all of the men in the groups were armed. Would that be correct? And you had --

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you had about ten rifles per group?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said more or less, about some ten rifles there were all together, including the ones that were homemade, the Kuburas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So when you say ten rifles all together, ten rifles all together in your group, would that be correct? We are not talking about all four groups.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think including the hunting weapons and the homemade weapons, yes, there were that many. Later, as the fighting progressed, of course, people got killed in order to obtain rifles. If we managed to capture some rifles, then the men who did not have any weapons would take the weapons and then they would continue to fight with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was exactly the purpose of my objection. The Prosecutor needs to specify when putting these questions, about the number of weapons, about which period she is asking for, in order that the witness does not get confused. But evidently he understood and he answered that particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time that is convenient for you, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can break now, and I'm leaning towards one break because I think we are moving much slower than I anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we go ahead for another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we have one break. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Registrar, correct me if I'm wrong, when we have one break only, usually we -- past half ten, until what time? Because I can't remember. We have the break at what time usually? I think it's quarter to, all right. So we go another 15 minutes and then we have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Your Honour. Just -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Getting back to the question about the weapons or the rifles, including those that were homemade, in what period of time did your group have about ten or so rifles? Are we talking in May, and June as well?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. June -- May, sorry, May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you managed to acquire more weapons in June?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was daily fighting, and our men were being killed as well as Serb men, when they were attacking us and of course we would seize some rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that there was hand-to-hand combat in these daily fightings?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And is this how you yourself managed to obtain a rifle?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly what -- where you were, what area you were fighting in, when you acquired this rifle?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the area of Velika Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So by July of 1992, approximately how many weapons would you say your group had?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of July or do you have the entire month in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's talk of it in terms of the period of the month. The end of July.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably around 15 to 20, somewhere in that region. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And in August, early part of August, and let me just specify: By the 8th of August, how many weapons did your group have?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps additional two or three rifles, and some got damaged, say, when a shrapnel would hit a rifle or so, and some got lost, too. Or, for example, a fighter of ours was killed and we couldn't pull out his body so his rifle remained behind as well. So the number of rifles changed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did the other three groups, the ones in the woods, Cizmici and Vladusici, did they also manage to acquire more weapons over the period of May, beginning of May, they had a few, I believe you said, about ten? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, it was happening the same way, changed slightly but on the same principle as with the group in Velika Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did they also manage to acquire more weapons over the period of time in the similar manner that your group did? When I say similar manner, I mean in fighting, if a soldier died, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain that they could -- that they were able to seize a larger number of weapons. We would usually seize one or two rifles. And if we seized one rifle, it would usually go to two men, and I'm not certain as to how they could have been able to seize greater numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the rifles that you were able to seize - your group, I'm referring to now - were they automatic, semi-automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few automatic and a few semi-automatic rifles. The Kuburas I mentioned, we didn't have enough ammunition for them. They used hunting ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it the other groups were also involved in hand-to-hand combat with the Serb in their areas during the month of May, June and July?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were two binoculars. Now, could you tell us which groups had the binoculars? You testified yesterday that a military binocular had been seized during one of the encounters with the Serbs and then there was a hunting binocular. Which group had the binoculars?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. I said a pair of binoculars was military and one was hunting binoculars, and those belonged to my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: He had them both?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a hunter and he had the hunting binoculars in his possession and we seized the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So your group had two binoculars?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One set of binoculars. And the other one was given to the other group. A person took the other a pair to Vladusici and the other pair of binoculars remained with our group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the persons who owned -- not owned, who used the binoculars, was it usually the same person or would different individuals use to reconnoiter the areas?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various, different people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you use them as well?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too often, or very little.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, as the leader of the group, what did Ejub Golic do with the information that was being given to him from the different groups?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would receive that information and he would pick a person to go to the other group, to tell them what was happening where, and then the other group would then send their person because they were more familiar with their area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would just like to briefly ask you about the different encounters that you had. When I say you, your group, had with the Serbs. Do you recall an encounter in Hranca in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have an encounter in Hranca at all?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. In July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were attacking us from that area. They were attacking us from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. But did you actually go into that area or have an encounter in the vicinity of Hranca?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about Polom [sic]?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was quite distant from where we were, Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about -- well, let me ask you this: What areas did you have the encounters in, your group?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velika Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It was only in Velika Glogova?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have our group in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, your group.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you travel outside of that particular area to an area of Veresinje?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about the other groups? Do you know if they themselves were engaging in contact with the Serbs during that period of time in that area? Fighters.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that. I can't say either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. But you yourself -- well, did you ever go to Veresinje?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: During 1992.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. And when was this?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to talk to you about the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a good time to take a break, actually, because I'm changing the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 30-minute break. Thank you. --- Break taken at 10.44 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about the -- moving to a different area, and ask you about the attack that took place on the 8th of August, of which you were involved in. Now, you testified yesterday that there was daily shelling in Cizmici and the shelling was from -- in particular with respect to Cizmici, that it was coming from Bezrani [phoen] and you also talked about the fact that Nurif Rizvanovic from Tuzla arrived with approximately 400 armed soldiers. Do you recall that testimony? And if you could just tell me yes or no, we do have a lot to cover, whether you recall.

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall but I didn't understand the name you mentioned, from what area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. You said you were being shelled from Cizmici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nurif Rizvanovic from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the direction they were shelling us from? That's what I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The time being is whether you recall having testified on this yesterday. That's all she wants to know. You remember testifying on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you recall - and you said that 400 armed men came with Mr. Nurif Rizvanovic and they were armed from Tuzla, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified that Mr. Rizvanovic and Dr. Mujkanovic was in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard -- yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And they had been there for three or four days before August 8th, correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Nurif Rizvanovic came to the area of Konjevic Polje and in amongst his group there was Dr. Mujkanovic, three to four days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let's do this. You need to be brief in your answer and I will ask you if you need to provide further explanation. If you just answer with a yes or no what I have stated to you, instead of repeating it, okay? So my next question is, you also stated that Nurif had been told by people who had -- who had been deported to Kladanj -- my colleague is assisting me with the pronunciation, Kladanj, and that your area was being shelled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What -- okay. What did -- what did the people from Kladanj tell Nurif Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that people from Glogova, on the 9th of May, that is a part of the people, were -- was collected by the Serbs and transferred to Kladanj and then they conveyed to Nurif Rizvanovic the situation, our situation, in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So it was from these deported individuals from Glogova that he learned what your situation was? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: (redacted) [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you further stated that on the 8th of August, that the people from Lunici -- Lolici, would that be the correct name, the people from --
